risks.title: The Phase 10 alert-metric gate silently drops any rule whose `expr:` precedes its `alert:` key
risks.evidence: Line 165 `alert = None`; line 176 `if match and alert:` — an `expr:` line is only yielded once an `alert:` line has already been seen in the same file. The function's own docstring at lines 152-164 promises the opposite: "Anything it cannot parse is reported, never skipped." The gate is wired at .github/workflows/ci.validate-alerts.yml:70 (`run: python tools/ci/check_alert_metrics.py`) and the file header calls it "the gate this phase exists to install: eleven metric names were alerted on that nothing in the repository produced."
risks.consequence: I reproduced this by loading the module and calling `_expressions()` on a two-rule file whose FIRST rule is written key-order `expr:` then `alert:` (valid YAML, valid PromQL, accepted by `promtool check rules`): input `- expr: totally_made_up_metric_total > 0` / `alert: FirstRuleExprFirst`, followed by a normal `- alert: SecondRule` / `expr: another_made_up_metric_total > 1`. Output was `[('SecondRule', 'another_made_up_metric_total > 1')]` — `totally_made_up_metric_total` was never returned, never tokenised, and never reported. So a new alert file (or a reordering of the first rule in an existing one) that references a metric no emitter produces passes ci.validate-alerts.yml green: `promtool check rules` accepts key order, `promtool test rules` only evaluates the alerts named in rule_tests.yaml, and check_alert_metrics.py exits 0. That is exactly the failure the gate was built to make impossible.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "CI gates: do they actually run, and do they actually gate?": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: Accurate version: `_expressions()` in tools/ci/check_alert_metrics.py silently drops the expression of any alert rule whose `expr` key is the first key of its list item, so the metrics it names are never tokenised and never reported. There are two independent causes, not the one the finding names: (1) the alert regex at line 172 is `\s*-?\s*alert:` and tolerates the YAML list dash, while the expr regex at line 175 is `(\s*)expr:` and does not — so `- expr: made_up_total > 0` never matches at all, even when `alert` has already been set by a previous rule (verified: a normal first rule followed by an expr-first second rule yields only the first rule's expression); (2) the `if match and alert:` guard at line 176 with `alert = None` at line 165 additionally drops any dashless expr line appearing before the file's first `alert:` line (reachable when the list dash sits on its own line). A file whose rules are all written expr-first yields zero expressions, not one dropped. This contradicts the function's own docstring at line 163 ("Anything it cannot parse is reported, never skipped") and is unguarded elsewhere: nothing in .github/ or tools/ enforces alert/expr key order, analyse() never reconciles the number of `alert:` keys against the number of extracted expressions, and `promtool test rules` evaluates only the alerts named in rule_tests.yaml — so such a rule passes ci.validate-alerts.yml green. Severity should be medium, not high: the bypass is latent, not live. No current rule file contains `- expr` (grep returns nothing) and extracted expressions match alert counts exactly today — application.yaml 4/4, platform.yaml 7/7, scan_lifecycle.yaml 6/6 — with the gate exiting 0 at "9 alert metric(s) emitted by the application, 9 declared external." The fix is one character plus one condition: `(\s*)-?\s*expr:` and dropping the `and alert` requirement (or reporting an expr with no known alert name rather than skipping it).

risks.title: The preview-deploy workflow builds the engine image without ENGINE_GIT_SHA, which this stack made a hard build-time requirement
risks.evidence:
engine/Dockerfile:10-11 (added by this stack; `git diff -- engine/Dockerfile` shows it as new):
    ARG ENGINE_GIT_SHA
    ENV ENGINE_GIT_SHA=${ENGINE_GIT_SHA}
    RUN python -c 'import os,re; assert re.fullmatch("[0-9a-f]{40}", os.environ.get("ENGINE_GIT_SHA", "")), "Build requires --build-arg ENGINE_GIT_SHA=<full source commit>"'

.github/workflows/pr.preview-deploy.yml:114-122 (tracked and unmodified by any phase - `git status .github/` lists nine changed workflow files and this is not one of them):
      - name: Build and push worker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: ./engine
          file: engine/Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: ${{ env.WORKER_IMAGE }}
          cache-from: type=gha,scope=worker
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max,scope=worker

No `build-args:` key. Every other place in the repository that builds this image supplies it: .github/workflows/ci.supply-chain.yml:53 (`--build-arg ENGINE_GIT_SHA=${{ github.sha }}`), tools/ci/container_smoke.py:52-54, docker-compose.production.yml:130 (`${ENGINE_GIT_SHA:?reviewed revision required}`).
risks.consequence: A maintainer adds the `deploy-preview` label to any pull request. The `build-images` job runs; BuildKit resolves `ARG ENGINE_GIT_SHA` to the empty string, `re.fullmatch("[0-9a-f]{40}", "")` returns None, the assert raises, the RUN layer exits non-zero and the "Build and push worker image" step fails. The `run-preview` job never starts and no preview is produced. README.md:56-62 asserts in one breath that pr.preview-deploy.yml is "the only registry push in the repository" and that ENGINE_GIT_SHA is something "the worker image refuses to build without" - the two statements together describe a workflow that cannot succeed.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "cross-phase consistency and integration coherence": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: Two corrections to the finding as stated, neither of which changes the verdict. (1) Line numbers: the Dockerfile block is at engine/Dockerfile:11-13, not 10-11 (line 9 is the `COPY --from=opa` and line 10 is blank). The pr.preview-deploy.yml citation at :114 is exact. (2) Severity is better placed at medium-high rather than high. The break is confined to the label-gated preview path: no required CI gate, no docker-compose.production.yml build, and no compliance evidence artifact routes through pr.preview-deploy.yml, so the impact is a developer-preview workflow that cannot succeed plus a README that asserts two mutually incompatible things at :55 and :58-59, not a production or audit-evidence failure. The one-line fix is a `build-args: ENGINE_GIT_SHA=${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` (falling back to github.sha on workflow_dispatch) on the "Build and push worker image" step.

risks.title: The preview-deploy workflow starts the API with APP_ENV=preview plus a dev database password and a plaintext Redis URL, which Phase 5's runtime validator rejects at import
risks.evidence:
.github/workflows/pr.preview-deploy.yml:266-280:
      - name: Start backend container
        run: |
          docker run -d \
            --name autoaudit-backend-api \
            ...
            -e APP_ENV=preview \
            -e DATABASE_URL=postgresql+asyncpg://autoaudit:autoaudit_dev_password@db:5432/autoaudit \
            ...
            -e REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379 \

backend-api/app/core/config.py validate_runtime_security (new in this stack - `git diff` shows the whole validator as added):
        if self.APP_ENV == "dev":
            return self
        if self.APP_ENV not in {"production", "prod", "staging", "preview", "test"}:
            ...
        def strong(value):
            return len(value) >= 32 and not any(
                marker in value.lower()
                for marker in ("change", "example", "password", "autoaudit_dev", "your-", "dev-secret"))
        ...
            or not strong(unquote(database.password or ""))
        ):
            raise ValueError("DATABASE_URL requires explicit database credentials outside dev")
        if (redis.scheme != "rediss" ...):
            raise ValueError("REDIS_URL requires authenticated TLS outside dev")

"preview" is in the allowed set, so the validator does NOT return early; it then evaluates the rest. `autoaudit_dev_password` is 21 characters and contains both "password" and "autoaudit_dev", so strong() is False on three counts. `redis://` is not `rediss://`.
risks.consequence: The preview backend container starts, runs backend-api/entrypoint.sh, which runs `alembic upgrade head`. backend-api/alembic/env.py:30,37 calls `get_settings()` at module import, Settings() raises ValidationError ("DATABASE_URL requires explicit database credentials outside dev"), alembic exits non-zero, `set -e` kills the entrypoint and the container exits before uvicorn is reached. The workflow's next step, "Wait for backend health" (line ~285), polls for 120 seconds and then fails. This is independent of CD-01: fixing the build arg would move the failure to this step.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "cross-phase consistency and integration coherence": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction:
The finding holds. Two small corrections and one scope clarification:

- The password `autoaudit_dev_password` is 22 characters, not 21 (still far below the 32-character floor, and it still matches two forbidden markers, so `strong()` is False on three counts as stated).
- The "Wait for backend health (includes Alembic migrations)" step is at line 283, not ~285. The offending env vars are at lines 272-276 within the step that begins at line 266.
- Scope: only the backend container is affected. The "Start worker container" step at line 312 uses the same weak `DATABASE_URL` and plaintext `REDIS_URL` (lines 321-322) but does **not** set `APP_ENV`, so `Settings.APP_ENV` falls back to its default `"dev"` (config.py:16) and `validate_runtime_security` returns early at config.py:126. The worker therefore starts; only `autoaudit-backend-api` dies.

On severity: the mechanism is certain and the whole preview-deploy job fails, but the blast radius is a label-triggered, opt-in ephemeral PR preview environment, not production or the default CI gate. Medium is a better fit than high.

risks.title: Criterion 1 not met: the release worktree is uncommitted and has never been integrated with an upstream main that is now 96 commits ahead
risks.evidence: `git status --short` in the worktree returns 380 entries (190 M, 178 ??, 12 D). Running the repository's own release tool, `python3 tools/ops/release_manifest.py`, returns `"source": {"revision": "8736fcb93565dcc1e1a60a06392a879f5a585335", "tree_clean": false}`. The branch `fix/soc2-phase-11-final-verification` has no commit of its own beyond 8736fcb9. `git rev-list --count 8736fcb9..upstream/main` = 96 and `git merge-base --is-ancestor 8736fcb9 upstream/main` reports "not ancestor"; upstream/main is 75b919d0 (2026-09-07), 24 commits beyond the 0a074cc9 that phase-10/verification.json records as upstream_main. docs/compliance/phase-10/verification.json's not_run list states verbatim: "Integration with current upstream main. Outstanding since Phase 7; upstream is now four revisions ahead."
risks.consequence: A release engineer takes the recorded release revision 8736fcb93565dcc1e1a60a06392a879f5a585335 and builds from it: they get the Phase 1 tree, not the ten phases of work being released, because none of it is committed. tools/ops/release_manifest.py's own docstring says ENGINE_GIT_SHA must equal the manifest revision for scan provenance to name the source it was built from, and with tree_clean=false that equality is meaningless. This is a code/state defect, not an external block: committing the tree and integrating upstream is engineering work that no third party gates.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Phase 11 release acceptance criteria (SOC2_EXECUTION_PLAN.md section 19.3, thirteen checkboxes)": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: Accurate version: SOC2_EXECUTION_PLAN.md section 19.3 criterion 1 ("Worktree and generated artifacts are controlled and reproducible") is not met, and the state is disclosed rather than concealed. The release worktree carries 380 uncommitted entries (190 M, 178 ??, 12 D). HEAD is 8736fcb93565dcc1e1a60a06392a879f5a585335, the Phase 1 containment commit, and every phase branch fix/soc2-phase-1-containment through fix/soc2-phase-10-production-operations points at that same commit, so nine phases of work exist only as working-tree state. Running the repository's own tools/ops/release_manifest.py yields revision 8736fcb9 with "tree_clean": false, and that tool's own comment at lines 121-122 states that "A manifest taken from a dirty tree does not describe a reproducible build". The manifest's revision/ENGINE_GIT_SHA equality requirement is stated in the emitted "note" field constructed at lines 124-127, not in the module docstring. The stack has also never been integrated with upstream: git rev-list --count 8736fcb9..upstream/main is 96 and 8736fcb9 is not an ancestor of upstream/main (75b919d0, 2026-09-07). Both facts are already recorded by the programme itself — docs/compliance/phase-10/verification.json's not_run list carries "Integration with current upstream main. Outstanding since Phase 7", every phase README states the branch is "uncommitted and unpushed; no PR", and Phase 11's own docs/compliance/phase-11/collisions.json quantifies the divergence (96 commits, 38 open PRs, 28 overlapping this stack, 478 files changed, 21 contended files). Partial mitigation exists in that docs/compliance/phase-11/phase-10-snapshot.json records SHA-256 for all 1004 files, which makes the tree byte-verifiable, but a digest list permits verification, not reconstruction from git. Only the local half of the remedy is ungated engineering work: committing the stack and rebasing it onto upstream/main. Landing it on upstream/main is gated by repo-owner PR review against 28 contending open PRs under plan rules 8 and 10, so the finding's "no third party gates" clause overstates the case. Severity is better characterised as an open, fully disclosed release blocker on criterion 1 rather than a hidden high-severity defect: Phase 11 has produced no README or verification.json yet and nothing in the tree asserts criterion 1 is satisfied, so reporting it as unmet is consistent with, not contradicted by, the phase's own artifacts.

risks.title: Criterion 11 not met: evidence is destructible on two API paths with no legal-hold check and no audit event
risks.evidence: backend-api/app/api/v1/scans.py:874-897 `delete_scan` executes `await db.execute(delete(ScanResult).where(ScanResult.scan_id == scan_id))` then `await db.delete(scan)` after only an ownership check — no legal_hold consultation, no evidence_audit event (grep for "audit" in scans.py returns one unrelated comment at line 141). backend-api/app/models/evidence_artifact.py:57,60 make scan_id and scan_result_id `ondelete="SET NULL"`, so a legally held artifact is silently orphaned rather than protecting the scan. Separately, backend-api/app/api/v1/manual_verification.py:164-182 `delete_manual_verification` does `await db.delete(detail)` with no audit write at all — its own module docstring at line 9 says "The audited replacement for this endpoint is app.api.v1.manual_evidence", yet the unaudited route is still registered. Both are recorded as open risks in docs/compliance/phase-10/README.md:442-446.
risks.consequence: An auditor applies a legal hold to the evidence artifact backing scan 42 via POST /v1/evidence/{id}/legal-hold (which correctly records legal_hold_applied). The scan owner then calls DELETE /api/v1/scans/42. Because evidence_artifact.scan_id is SET NULL and delete_scan never reads legal_hold, the scan row and every ScanResult row — the provenance, policy digest, input digest and outcome that the report→mapping→result→policy→collector→evidence trace depends on — are permanently deleted, the held artifact is orphaned from the result it evidenced, and no audit event of any kind is written. The hold that exists precisely to survive the data owner's wish to delete does not survive it.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Phase 11 release acceptance criteria (SOC2_EXECUTION_PLAN.md section 19.3, thirteen checkboxes)": survived 3 independent refuters (1 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction:
Accurate version (severity: low-to-medium, ergonomics/audit gap, not evidence destruction):

`DELETE /api/v1/scans/{scan_id}` (backend-api/app/api/v1/scans.py:875-897) performs only an ownership check and writes no evidence_audit event, and it makes no attempt to handle the FK consequences of the delete. When any `evidence_artifact` row references the scan or its results, the `ondelete="SET NULL"` referential update fires the `phase7_artifact_identity_immutable` BEFORE UPDATE trigger (alembic/versions/f7d2c48b1a03_phase7_audit_evidence.py:306-330), which raises ERRCODE 23514; when approved manual evidence exists, the `ondelete="RESTRICT"` FKs (app/models/manual_evidence.py:105-111) raise instead. Neither is caught, so the endpoint answers 500 rather than a deliberate 409 explaining that held or approved evidence blocks the delete. The evidence itself is preserved — the finding's claim that a legally held artifact is silently orphaned is false.

The real, narrower gaps are: (1) `delete_scan` never consults `EvidenceArtifact.legal_hold` explicitly, so the protection is incidental to a schema trigger rather than an intentional, testable guard, and the failure surfaces as an opaque 500; (2) neither `delete_scan` nor `delete_manual_verification` (app/api/v1/manual_verification.py:163-181) writes any audit event, and the latter remains registered (app/api/v1/router.py:54) alongside its own documented audited replacement. Both are already recorded as accepted open risks in docs/compliance/phase-10/README.md:442-447, so if Phase 11 carries them into its risk register with an owner they are handled items rather than new defects; if the Phase 11 register omits them, the finding to raise is the omission, not evidence destructibility.

risks.title: Deleting an evidence artifact leaves an encrypted excerpt of the same evidence in evidence_validation, a table with no retention, no hold, no audit trail and no deletion path
risks.evidence: EvidenceValidation declares `source_filename`, `text_hash`, `extracted_text_encrypted` ("Optional encrypted extracted text (or excerpt) for secure traceability") and `matches_json`, and declares no retention_policy_version, no retention_expires_at, no legal_hold and no deleted_at — unlike EvidenceArtifact (models/evidence_artifact.py:86-89). It is written at evidence.py:1437-1449 during POST /v1/evidence/scan with `extracted_text_encrypted=_encrypt_excerpt(text)`. `grep -rn EvidenceValidation --include='*.py' .` shows the class is referenced only by the model, __init__, the schema, alembic/env.py and that one construction site: no route reads it and no statement anywhere deletes it. delete_artifact (evidence.py:1063-1146) touches only the artifact row and its storage key. Phase 10's own key-rotation note calls the column "retained evidence" (docs/compliance/phase-10/README.md) and its recorded gap list names only the drift and factprint tables as retention-less.
risks.consequence: A tenant uploads a document through POST /v1/evidence/scan, then exercises DELETE /v1/evidence/artifacts/{object_id}. The API returns 204, the bytes are unlinked and verified gone (:1112-1116), and the row is tombstoned with a `deleted` audit event. The encrypted excerpt of the same document's extracted text, its original filename and the validator match JSON remain in evidence_validation for ever, under no retention policy, reachable by any holder of the encryption key ring, with no audit event recording that they still exist and no code path that can remove them. The endpoint's own docstring — "Soft-delete: the row survives as a tombstone, the bytes do not" — is therefore not true of all copies of the evidence content.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.11 — evidence ownership, approval, retention, expiry, deletion, and report access": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: The finding stands; two details should be tightened. (1) File path: the route code is backend-api/app/api/v1/evidence.py (not backend-api/app/routers/evidence.py), though every cited line number in that file is exact. (2) "no audit event recording that they still exist" is slightly overstated: evidence.py:1451-1453 writes provenance["evidence_validation_id"] onto the artifact row, so the tombstone that survives DELETE does carry a durable pointer to the orphaned validation row. That pointer is an artifact column only — it never enters an evidence_audit_event detail, and no code path acts on it — so the substance (no retention, no hold, no audit event, no deletion path) is unchanged; the row is merely discoverable, not manageable. Also worth strengthening: "excerpt" understates the exposure, since _MAX_ENCRYPTED_EXCERPT_CHARS = 20000 (evidence.py:121) means the stored ciphertext is the entire extracted text for most uploaded documents; and the FK created in alembic/versions/f6c7d8e9f012 has no ON DELETE clause, so not even deleting the owning user can remove these rows. On documentation status: Phase 10's gap list does record the general statement "Retention exists only for evidence_artifact" (docs/compliance/phase-10/README.md:454), which partially covers the retention half of this finding, but it names only the drift and factprint tables and nowhere records that DELETE /v1/evidence/artifacts/{object_id} leaves a copy of the evidence text behind. Severity high is appropriate for a SOC 2 evidence-lifecycle context, with the mitigation that the text is stored encrypted and is unreachable through any API route.

risks.title: The legal-hold endpoint's stated control ("the owner cannot lift their own") is not implemented: an owner with the auditor or admin role can release the hold on their own evidence and then delete it
risks.evidence: The docstring at evidence.py:1687-1690 states: "**Auditor or admin, not the owner.** A hold has to survive the data owner's wish to delete -- that is what distinguishes it from ordinary retention -- so the owner cannot lift their own. The lookup is therefore deliberately not ownership-scoped". The handler's only authorization is `current_user: User = Depends(require_auditor_or_above)` (:1682), and app/core/permissions.py:38-45 checks nothing but the global `user.role in [admin, auditor]`. The row lookup at :1698-1710 filters on object_id and status only. There is no comparison of `current_user.id` against `artifact.user_id` anywhere in the handler, and no database constraint equivalent to `ck_manual_evidence_record_independent_reviewer` (migration line 209-213), which is exactly how the same separation of duties is enforced for manual-evidence approvals.
risks.consequence: User U has role='auditor' (roles are a single global column, models/user.py:19-24, and Phase 10 records that no API route writes user.role, so a role is assigned out of band and never revisited). Auditor V places a hold on U's artifact A. U posts {"hold": false, "reason": "no longer required"} to /v1/evidence/artifacts/A/legal-hold — require_auditor_or_above passes because U is an auditor, and the deliberately non-ownership-scoped lookup finds U's own artifact. The hold is released, an audit event records U as the actor, and U then calls DELETE /v1/evidence/artifacts/A, which passes the :1089 gate and destroys the bytes. The data owner has lifted their own hold, which is the precise thing the docstring says cannot happen.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.11 — evidence ownership, approval, retention, expiry, deletion, and report access": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: Accurate version (severity: medium, kind: code-defect / untrue in-code claim): The legal-hold endpoint (backend-api/app/api/v1/evidence.py:1679-1740) does not enforce separation of duties between the hold's subject and the actor releasing it, so its docstring claim at :1687-1690 that "the owner cannot lift their own" is true only for owners whose global role is 'viewer'. The sole authorization is require_auditor_or_above (:1682), which checks nothing but user.role (app/core/permissions.py:38-45), and the lookup (:1698-1710) is deliberately not ownership-scoped. An artifact owner who also holds the auditor or admin role can therefore POST {"hold": false, ...} to /v1/evidence/artifacts/{id}/legal-hold on their own artifact and then DELETE it, since delete_artifact's only remaining gate is `if artifact.legal_hold` at :1089 (its lookup at :1075 is owner-scoped and its auth at :1067 is bare get_current_user, and uploads are likewise get_current_user, so auditors do own artifacts). No structural guard equivalent to ck_manual_evidence_record_independent_reviewer (alembic/versions/f7d2c48b1a03_phase7_audit_evidence.py:211-214) exists for legal hold, and no test exercises the endpoint's authority at all. Severity is medium rather than high because the actor must already hold a privileged role — an ordinary user cannot do this — and both the release and the delete are recorded with actor_user_id in the append-only, UPDATE/DELETE-forbidden evidence audit trail, so the act is attributable after the fact. Note also that docs/compliance/phase-10/README.md:513 already asks security/GRC to "confirm that auditor-or-above is the right authority for applying a legal hold ... since neither is ownership-scoped"; that partially covers the authority model but does not state the self-release case, so the unqualified docstring claim remains untrue of the code.

risks.title: An approved manual-evidence bundle's attachments can be destroyed unilaterally by the submitter after approval; approval places no hold and writes no revision
risks.evidence: delete_artifact authorizes on ownership plus `if artifact.legal_hold` (evidence.py:1075-1089) and nothing else — it never consults manual_evidence_revision.attachment_object_ids. `grep -rn legal_hold backend-api/app` shows legal_hold appears in no manual-evidence file, so approve_record (api/v1/manual_evidence.py:423-446 -> services/manual_evidence.py:apply_transition) places no hold on the artifacts it just digested into `evidence_sha256` (services/manual_evidence.py:267-286). The record's own FKs are deliberately `ondelete="RESTRICT"` with the comment "approved evidence must not be silently destroyed by deleting a scan. Deletion has to go through the audited path" (models/manual_evidence.py:104-112), but no equivalent protection exists on the artifact side. soc2.py:398-421 `_approved_manual_evidence` selects on `status == 'approved'` only.
risks.consequence: Submitter U attaches artifacts A and B, submits, and reviewer V approves; revision N records evidence_sha256 over {A,B} and the record goes to status 'approved'. U then calls DELETE /v1/evidence/artifacts/A and DELETE /v1/evidence/artifacts/B. Both succeed (U owns them, legal_hold is false). The manual_evidence_record stays 'approved' with reviewer_user_id and reviewed_at intact, no new revision is written, and GET /v1/soc2/{scan_id}/soc2-report continues to report the control as backed by approved manual evidence — while the approved bundle's bytes no longer exist and cannot be produced to an auditor. Plan section 15.4's guard, "Do not make approved evidence directly editable or deletable without an audit event", is satisfied only in the narrow sense that the evidence router logs the deletion; the approval record itself is silently hollowed out.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.11 — evidence ownership, approval, retention, expiry, deletion, and report access": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: Accurate version: Approval of a manual-evidence record places no retention protection on the artifacts it digests. delete_artifact (backend-api/app/api/v1/evidence.py:1063-1114) authorizes on ownership alone (_owned_artifact, lines 437-447) plus `artifact.legal_hold` (line 1089); it never consults manual_evidence_revision.attachment_object_ids (a plain JSONB column, models/manual_evidence.py:206, with no FK). approve_record (api/v1/manual_evidence.py:423-443 -> services/manual_evidence.py apply_transition) sets no hold, and revalidation of attachment availability is scoped to submit/approve only (services/manual_evidence.py:80-84, resolve_attachments 287-308). Consequently a submitter can, after approval, DELETE /v1/evidence/artifacts/{id} for every attachment in the approved bundle; the record stays 'approved' with reviewer_user_id and reviewed_at intact, no revision is written, and GET /v1/soc2/{scan_id}/soc2-report (soc2.py:398-419, 468) keeps reporting the control as backed by approved manual evidence with no attachment/availability field to signal otherwise. Corrections to the original wording: (1) the deletion is NOT silent in absolute terms — an append-only evidence_audit_event with action 'deleted' is recorded and the artifact row survives as a status='deleted' tombstone, so the loss is discoverable from the evidence audit trail even though nothing in the manual-evidence record or the SOC 2 report reflects it; (2) plan section 15.4's guard as literally written ("Do not make approved evidence directly editable or deletable without an audit event") IS satisfied, so this should be filed against Phase 11 item 19.1.11 (evidence approval/retention/deletion) rather than as a 15.4 violation; (3) severity is better rated medium than high: it requires the authenticated submitter to act, it is fully audited, the artifact tombstone remains, and the deliberate mechanism (legal_hold, exposed as set_legal_hold at evidence.py:1679 in Phase 10) exists and can be applied — the gap is that nothing applies it automatically at approval and no phase handoff documents that as a decision.

risks.title: The SOC 2 report is owner-scoped only; the auditor role that gates cross-owner review elsewhere is not applied to it
risks.evidence: `select(Scan).where(Scan.id == scan_id, Scan.user_id == current_user.id)` — the sole authorization in get_soc2_report, followed by a 404 when it misses. There is no role branch anywhere in the module (`grep -n "require_auditor_or_above|require_admin" backend-api/app/api/v1/soc2.py` returns nothing). Yet Role.AUDITOR exists (backend-api/app/models/user.py:22), require_auditor_or_above is defined (backend-api/app/core/permissions.py:38-45) and is applied to cross-owner surfaces: manual_evidence.py:119 (review-queue, which explicitly selects rows where `ManualEvidenceRecord.user_id != current_user.id`), manual_evidence.py:428 and :452, drift.py:156 and :221, evidence.py:1682 and :1753 (the evidence access log).
risks.consequence: A GRC reviewer is provisioned with role='auditor' as the rest of the system intends, and is asked to perform the 19.1.12 trace on scan 42, run by an engineer. `GET /v1/scans/42/soc2-report` returns 404 Not Found — indistinguishable from the scan not existing. The same reviewer CAN see that engineer's submitted manual evidence through /manual-evidence/review-queue and CAN read the evidence access log, so the asymmetry is not a considered privacy posture but an omission. The only routes to the report are (a) the scan owner logs in and hands over a JSON blob, or (b) someone runs SQL against the production database. Phase-10 README:512 asks GRC to 'confirm that auditor-or-above is the right authority for applying a legal hold and reading the evidence access log' and is silent on the report, so no phase has recorded a decision to keep this owner-only.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.12 — GRC traceability chain (report → mapping → result → policy → collector → normalized evidence → source/provenance) and existence of a SOC 2 evidence-pack generator": survived 3 independent refuters (1 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction:
Two amendments; the core defect stands.

(1) "No phase has recorded a decision to keep this owner-only" is too strong. The endpoint's own docstring (soc2.py:474-478) states "Owner-authorized. A scan belonging to another user is a 404, not a 403, so the endpoint does not confirm that a scan id exists", and phase-7/README.md:73-74 documents the same ownership+404 non-enumeration pattern for the evidence store. So the owner-scoping and the 404-over-403 choice ARE documented; what is undocumented is any weighing of auditor access to the report. It is an unconsidered question, not an undocumented behaviour — and, unlike evidence.py:1682/:1753, no docstring here justifies excluding the auditor role.

(2) Add a corroborating detail that enlarges the fix: soc2.py:505 passes current_user.id into _drift_stream -> drift.soc2_drift_summary -> _latest_run_for_scan (services/drift.py:687), which filters DriftRun.user_id == user_id. Swapping the dependency to require_auditor_or_above alone would give a non-owning auditor a report whose drift stream silently reports available:false — a materially different document from the one the owner sees. The fix must decouple the drift read's user scope from the caller as well.

(3) Severity: medium, not high. The endpoint fails closed (no cross-tenant leak, no privilege escalation; admins are equally excluded), and phase-11 traceability-trace.md:7-8 already grants the reviewer "a database connection and an authenticated API session". The concrete impact is that trace's own table row "report -> mapping | yes" (traceability-trace.md, "What a GRC reviewer can and cannot do unaided") is true only for the scan owner: an auditor-role reviewer gets a 404 indistinguishable from a nonexistent scan, and the trace never records that constraint.

risks.title: The SOC 2 report does not identify the tenant it describes
risks.evidence: Soc2Provenance (schemas/soc2.py:110-131), whose docstring reads "Everything needed to reproduce this document from frozen inputs", publishes `connection_snapshot_present: bool = False` and no tenant identity. soc2.py:599 populates it as `connection_snapshot_present=scan.connection_snapshot is not None`. The tenant_id is frozen on the scan at creation (backend-api/app/api/v1/scans.py:322-334 writes connection_snapshot={'tenant_id': ..., 'client_id': ..., ...}) but the report never reads it. The report also omits m365_connection_id; and the scan detail endpoint deliberately publishes only field NAMES (scans.py:579 `connection_snapshot_fields=sorted(...)`), never values.
risks.consequence: A GRC reviewer is handed two soc2-report JSON documents from a deployment that scans several customer tenants. Nothing in either document says which Microsoft 365 tenant it covers — the reports are distinguishable only by scan_id. To answer "which tenant is this report about?" the reviewer must issue two further owner-scoped API calls (GET /v1/scans/{id} for m365_connection_id, then the m365-connections endpoint for tenant_id) or run SQL against scan.connection_snapshot. For an audit deliverable this is the single most load-bearing fact about the document, and the class docstring's claim that the block contains everything needed to reproduce the document is false with respect to its subject.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.12 — GRC traceability chain (report → mapping → result → policy → collector → normalized evidence → source/provenance) and existence of a SOC 2 evidence-pack generator": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction:
The SOC 2 report response body carries no identifier for the M365 connection or tenant it describes. `Soc2Provenance` (backend-api/app/schemas/soc2.py:110-131) publishes only `connection_snapshot_present: bool` (line 129, populated at backend-api/app/api/v1/soc2.py:599), and no other part of the response — header (soc2.py:546-570), totals, drift_stream — carries `m365_connection_id`, `connection_name`, or the `connection_identity_digest` that already exists in backend-api/app/services/drift.py:241. Two reports from a deployment scanning several tenants are therefore distinguishable within the document only by `scan_id`.

Severity: MEDIUM, not high, for three reasons. (a) Attribution is one call away, not two: `GET /v1/scans/{scan_id}` (scans.py:496, response_model `ScanRead`) returns both `m365_connection_id` and `connection_name` (schemas/scan.py:60-61; the property is models/compliance.py:130-135), so only the raw tenant GUID requires the m365-connections endpoint. (b) The report exists solely as an owner-scoped JSON response addressed by scan_id — Phase 11's own traceability-trace.md:22-23 records that no durable evidence-pack artifact is written anywhere — so the "two detached documents" scenario is not one the system currently produces; the gap becomes load-bearing the moment a pack export is added. (c) The claim that the class docstring "Everything needed to reproduce this document from frozen inputs" is false does not hold: reproduction re-renders from the pinned mapping/metadata/result digests keyed by scan_id, and no field of the document derives from tenant identity. The block is incomplete as to the document's subject, not as to its reproducibility.

Also note the finding's own remedy must respect an existing deliberate invariant: withholding raw tenant/client values from API responses is documented in code (schemas/scan.py:238; scans.py:578) and enforced by test (backend-api/tests/test_phase7_soc2.py:1321-1322, `assert "synthetic" not in json.dumps(provenance)`). The correct fix is a surrogate — `m365_connection_id` and/or `connection_identity_digest` in `Soc2Provenance` — not the tenant GUID. Finally, the finding mislocates scans.py:579: that line belongs to `get_scan_provenance` (`GET /{scan_id}/provenance`, declared scans.py:524), not to the scan detail endpoint.

Accurate version: CIS 2.1.12 (line 48), 2.1.13 (line 49) and 2.1.14 (line 52) each build a correct three-valued helper (true / false / null-for-unknown) and then collapse it with `<helper> == true`, which in Rego is a defined `false` for the null case. That ValueError is classified by engine/worker/tasks.py:145 `return not isinstance(exc, ValueError)` — i.e. NOT retryable — so the retry branch at tasks.py:500 `if retryable and not exhausted:` is skipped and the terminal branch writes the error row on attempt 1. The design premise for that classification is stated at tasks.py:78-83 ("a collector error envelope" is a failure "a retry cannot change") and locked in by engine/tests/test_phase9_execution_plan.py:270 `test_an_error_envelope_is_a_group_failure_and_is_not_retried`, whose worked example is a genuinely deterministic absent-role envelope. This collector breaks that premise by putting transient transport failures into the same envelope. engine/collectors/entra/applications/forms_settings.py:68 has the identical `collector_error = str(exc)` pattern. No test covers the fallback branch: grep for `microsoft365Apps` across engine/tests returns nothing.

An identical 429 storm against any other Graph control (e.g. entra.groups.groups) propagates an httpx.HTTPStatusError, is classified retryable at tasks.py:135 (429 is not in NON_RETRYABLE_STATUS at :116), and gets three further attempts at 60s intervals. 1.3.4 is one of the 44 Appendix B crosswalk controls, so a throttle that every other Appendix B control rides out silently costs coverage on this one. risks.title: CIS 2.1.8 and 2.1.10 raise a builtin type error on the ordinary non-compliant case, so a real SPF/DMARC violation is recorded as 'error' and these controls can never return 'failed'
risks.evidence: spf_record_published(domain) if { record := trim(domain.spf_record, " \t\r\n"); record != ""; startswith(lower(record), "v=spf1") }. engine/collectors/exchange/dns/dns_security_records.py:60-61 initialises spf_record and dmarc_record to None and leaves them None when the lookup finds nothing (NXDOMAIN/NoAnswer/timeout are recorded in spf_error, which the policy never reads). Run with the exact flags evaluate_snapshot uses (--fail --strict-builtin-errors) on {"domains":[{"domain":"contoso.com","spf_record":null,"spf_error":"DNS query timeout"}]}: exit 2, "trim: operand 1 must be string but got null", code eval_type_error. The same run against 2.1.10 gives "lower: operand 1 must be string but got null" at 2.1.10_DMARC_records_published.rego:48.
risks.consequence: A tenant domain genuinely has no SPF record — the exact condition CIS 2.1.8 exists to detect. The collector sets spf_record=None, the policy calls trim(null), --strict-builtin-errors makes that a hard OPA failure, opa_client raises, and the control is stored as status='error' with reason_code='evaluation_error' after three full re-collections. Combined with F7 (empty domain list -> pass), controls 2.1.8 and 2.1.10 have only two reachable outcomes in practice: 'passed' and 'error'. A true finding is therefore never reported as a finding, and it drops out of both the compliance numerator and denominator instead.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.8 / acceptance criterion "unknown/error results cannot appear as pass or ordinary noncompliance"": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: The defect is real as described at both named lines; only the closing generalisation needs narrowing. Accurate version: "CIS 2.1.8 and 2.1.10 raise a builtin type error when a domain has no SPF/DMARC record — the exact condition the controls exist to detect — so a real violation is recorded as status='error' with reason_code='evaluation_error' instead of 'failed'. The collector (engine/collectors/exchange/dns/dns_security_records.py:60-61) leaves spf_record/dmarc_record as None whenever the lookup finds nothing (the reason goes to spf_error/dmarc_error, which neither policy reads), and evaluate_snapshot's --strict-builtin-errors turns trim(null) at 2.1.8:45 and lower(null) at 2.1.10:48 into a hard OPA exit-2 failure. Because tasks.py:139-142 classifies evaluation_error as retryable under max_retries=3, this costs three full re-collections per affected control before the error row is written, and result_contract.py:37-50 excludes 'error' from both the compliance numerator and denominator. Reachable outcomes: control 2.1.8 has only 'passed' and 'error' — the collector only ever stores a string already beginning with v=spf1, which always satisfies the rule, so 'failed' is unreachable for 2.1.8 in production. Control 2.1.10 can still return 'failed', but only in the narrow case where every tenant domain has a published v=DMARC1 record and at least one uses a non-enforcing p= value (verified: p=none returns compliant:false, exit 0); a single domain with no DMARC record poisons the evaluation for the entire domain list. No test in engine/tests exercises either policy." Severity: medium is defensible, but high is arguably more accurate for 2.1.8, since it is a CIS control marked severity: high in its own METADATA whose only true-positive outcome is structurally unreachable.

    COPY --chown=appuser:appuser mappings/ ./mappings/

risks.title: A failed or throttled sub-request in the Intune device-management collector is silently published as a zero count in CIS 4.1 evidence
risks.evidence: device_management_settings.py:36-42: `try: compliance_settings = await client.get("/deviceManagement/deviceCompliancePolicySettingStateSummaries", beta=True)` / `except Exception: compliance_settings = {}`, then at :49 `"compliance_policy_summaries": compliance_settings.get("value", [])`. The bare `except Exception` swallows every failure GraphClient can raise after its own bounded retry — 429, 403, 500, timeout, connection reset — and emits an empty list with no error marker, no `collector_error` key and no distinguishing field. Because nothing in the returned dict signals failure, engine/worker/tasks.py:887-893 does not raise, the collection is treated as successful, `factprint` is computed at :913 and the result is written as a normal assessment. The value is published in the audit record: engine/policies/cis/microsoft-365-foundations/v6.0.0/4.1_mark_unmanaged_devices_not_compliant.rego:51 emits `"compliance_policy_summaries_count": count(input.compliance_policy_summaries)`. This is the only consumer (grep for `compliance_policy_summaries` across engine/policies returns exactly that one line). CIS 4.1 is `automation_status: ready` with `data_collector_id: entra.devices.device_management_settings` in v6.0.0/metadata.json. No test drives this collector's failing sub-request — the collector is absent from the GRAPH_CASES matrix in engine/tests/test_phase4_collector_contracts.py.
risks.consequence: The tenant throttles the second Graph call: `/deviceManagement/settings` returns 200 with `secureByDefault: true, isScheduledActionEnabled: true`, and `/deviceManagement/deviceCompliancePolicySettingStateSummaries` returns 429 four times, exhausting GraphClient's retry. The exception is swallowed at :41 and CIS 4.1 is recorded `passed` with details `compliance_policy_summaries_count: 0`, byte-identical to the record produced for a tenant that genuinely has zero compliance policy summaries. An auditor reading the stored provenance and details cannot tell a throttled read from a real zero, and no retry is attempted for the missing half of the evidence. The verdict itself is not falsified (the rego at :28-31 keys only on secure_by_default and is_scheduled_action_enabled), which is why this is low rather than high — but it is a failed collection presented as evidence, which is what plan rule 5 in section 2 forbids. CIS 4.1 is not one of the 44 Appendix B controls, so it is not covered by the 19.3 contract-coverage criterion.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.10 — broker failure, task redelivery, concurrent finalization, cancellation, tenant mismatch, throttling, PowerShell rejection": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction:
The finding holds as stated; three refinements to its framing, none of which change the verdict or the low severity.

(a) Plan rule 5 ("Missing, incomplete, unauthorized, truncated, or failed collection must never become `pass`") is only weakly engaged. The `pass`/`fail` verdict for CIS 4.1 is derived entirely from `/deviceManagement/settings`, which succeeded; the swallowed sub-request feeds only a details field. The real defect is evidential fidelity, not verdict integrity: an incomplete collection is recorded as a complete one, and `compliance_policy_summaries_count: 0` is byte-identical for a throttled read and a true zero. Rule 6 (a failed collection must not be represented as tenant state; use an explicit indeterminate or error state) is the closer fit.

(b) Scope context worth recording: the file is pre-existing legacy, untouched by the SOC 2 programme — `git status --porcelain` is clean for it and its last commits are 381b1e58 "Implement Graph API based collectors for v6" / ce831020 "Collectors IP". CIS 4.1 sits outside the 44-control Appendix B population that phases 4 and 9 hardened, so this is a gap in un-scoped code rather than a regression introduced or a claim falsified by any phase handoff. It is a type (a) code defect, not a type (b) or (c) finding.

(c) The fix is one line and has an in-tree pattern: bind the exception and return a `collector_error` key as `forms_settings.py` and `apps_and_services_settings.py` do, which tasks.py:887-893 already checks. Alternatively, if the sub-request is genuinely intended as supplementary, the minimum is an explicit rationale comment plus a distinguishable value (e.g. `None` rather than `[]`), following the documented precedent at `e8_mfa_enforcement.py:161-163`.

risks.title: The SOC 2 report omits the result message and affected-resource count that are stored on the row and published elsewhere
risks.evidence: Soc2ControlEvidence (schemas/soc2.py:134-153) has control_id, title, in_benchmark, in_scan, selected, status, reason_code, automation_status and provenance — and no `message` or `evidence` field. soc2.py:_control_evidence (lines 341-386) never reads result.message or result.evidence. Both columns exist and are populated: engine/worker/tasks.py:337-338 writes message=MESSAGES[status] and evidence={'affected_resource_count': len(validated.affected_resources)}, and ScanResultRead (backend-api/app/schemas/scan.py:47-48) publishes both on GET /v1/scans/{id}/results. The withholding rule the module documents (soc2.py:80-92) is about provenance.policy_source and collected tenant payloads; an integer count is neither.
risks.consequence: CIS 1.1.3 fails on a tenant with six global administrators. The SOC 2 report tells the reviewer status='failed' and reason_code='policy_violation' and stops there — it does not say how many resources were affected, even though the number 6 is sitting in scan_result.evidence. The reviewer must make a second, separately-authorized call to GET /v1/scans/{id}/results to obtain a datum the report already had in hand, which weakens the report's standing as the self-contained document item 19.1.12 asks GRC to trace from.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.12 — GRC traceability chain (report → mapping → result → policy → collector → normalized evidence → source/provenance) and existence of a SOC 2 evidence-pack generator": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: Accurate version, severity low (arguably informational): the SOC 2 report's per-control evidence omits the affected-resource count. Soc2ControlEvidence (backend-api/app/schemas/soc2.py:134-153) has no `evidence` field, and _control_evidence (backend-api/app/api/v1/soc2.py:335-377) never reads result.evidence, even though engine/worker/tasks.py:338 stores {"affected_resource_count": N} on every assessed row and GET /v1/scans/{id}/results publishes it to the same owner. Drop the `message` half of the finding entirely: MESSAGES (engine/worker/tasks.py:303-307) is a static per-status string, so it is fully determined by the `status` the report already carries, and backend-api/app/api/v1/soc2.py:84 names "messages" among what the module excludes by default. Drop the "separately-authorized call" framing: both endpoints share the same get_current_user dependency and the same owner filter, so this is a second call to the same API under the same authorization, not a second authorization. The residual gap is that no phase document states a decision on the affected-resource count either way, while a count derived from collected tenant data is plausibly covered by the module's existing rule against publishing collected payloads in the report; the right remedy is a one-line documented decision, not necessarily a schema change.

risks.title: The evaluator is identified in provenance only by a self-reported version string; the pinned OPA image digest never reaches the scan row
risks.evidence: tasks.py:934 `provenance["opa_version"] = runtime_version` and :956 `opa_version=evaluated.opa_version`, both sourced from `opa.runtime().version` inside the evaluated query (engine/opa_client.py:131, 155) — a string the binary reports about itself. engine/Dockerfile:1 does pin the evaluator by content: `FROM openpolicyagent/opa:1.20.2@sha256:7b15f9d96345dfa639322ad97f65a0b38260f95efcdd7f5c24e284228708f06c`, but that digest is never recorded in provenance. The only content-addressed slot is engine_image_digest (provenance.py:83), which is optional and set nowhere: grepping docker-compose.yml, docker-compose.production.yml, env.example, engine/Dockerfile and infrastructure/ for ENGINE_IMAGE_DIGEST returns no match, while ENGINE_GIT_SHA is required in both compose files. engine_source_digest (provenance.py:70-86) covers only opa_client.py, worker/*.py and collectors/**/*.py — not the OPA binary, not the Python interpreter, not engine/uv.lock.
risks.consequence: Set OPA_BINARY (worker/config.py:51) to a locally built or patched `opa` that reports version '1.20.2'. Every result row records opa_version '1.20.2' and engine_image_digest null, indistinguishable from the digest-pinned image, and a reproducer following the row has no stored value that names which binary actually decided the outcome.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.9 — a complete scan can be reproduced from stored provenance": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: The finding stands; one detail in the evidence is mis-stated. It says both values are "sourced from opa.runtime().version inside the evaluated query". Only the value at tasks.py:956 comes from inside the query (engine/opa_client.py:131 builds '{"result": data.<pkg>.result, "opa_version": opa.runtime().version}', read back at :155). The value at tasks.py:934 comes from a separate invocation, opa_client.runtime_version() (opa_client.py:102-108, `opa eval --format=json opa.runtime().version`), called once at tasks.py:916 before the per-control loop. Both are still the binary reporting its own version, so the substance is unchanged. Worth adding for precision: engine_image_digest is the *engine worker image* digest, not an OPA-specific slot (documented as optional for standalone image deployments at docs/compliance/phase-3/README.md:123); recording it would content-address the image containing the pinned OPA binary but would still not name the OPA image digest directly. Also note the absence of any runtime guard — engine/worker_entrypoint.sh checks only `opa version >/dev/null`, and the 1.20.2 pin is asserted only in CI (tools/ci/integration_requirements.py:26).

risks.title: not_assessable and pre-dispatch error rows carry no engine identity and no record of the setting that produced them
risks.evidence: initial_provenance (provenance.py:89-119) returns engine_git_sha=None and engine_image_digest=None and omits engine_source_digest and engine_worktree_dirty as keys entirely. engine/worker/tasks.py:228-241 writes exactly that record for reason codes 'automation_disabled', 'not_automated', 'metadata_control_missing' and 'collector_not_configured'. The 'automation_disabled' branch is decided by `powershell_enabled` (tasks.py:50-54): `return settings.ENABLE_POWERSHELL_CONTROLS or not uses_powershell(collector_id)` — neither the setting's value nor the routing table's version is recorded anywhere on the row.
risks.consequence: A scan finishes with 22 controls `not_assessable`/`automation_disabled`. Those 22 sit in the coverage denominator and depress the reported automated coverage, yet the rows record no engine_git_sha, no engine_source_digest and no configuration value. A reproducer cannot determine which build's collectors.routing table classified those collector ids as PowerShell, so the 'not assessable' verdict — a substantive scan outcome, not merely an absence — cannot be re-derived without assuming an engine version. Phase 3 documents that non-executed results carry 'explicit null execution fields', which covers the timestamps and digests; it does not address the identity of the engine that made the decision.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.9 — a complete scan can be reproduced from stored provenance": survived 3 independent refuters (0 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction:
Accurate version: in a mixed scan the engine build is not wholly unrecoverable — every executed row in the same scan carries `engine_git_sha` and `engine_source_digest` (written from `engine_identity()` at tasks.py:797), and `collectors/routing.py` is inside that source digest, so a reproducer can usually infer which routing table applied by reading a sibling row (assuming one worker build served the whole scan — not guaranteed under a rolling deploy). The claim holds unconditionally only in the degenerate case where every selected control is `not_assessable`/error, leaving the scan with no row carrying engine identity at all.

The genuinely unrecoverable half is the configuration value: `settings.ENABLE_POWERSHELL_CONTROLS` is read once (tasks.py:54) and persisted nowhere in any provenance record, scan column or snapshot, so an `automation_disabled` verdict cannot be re-derived from stored data even when the engine build is known. Severity low is right, and kind criterion-not-met (19.1.9) is right, but the finding is better stated as "the deciding configuration value is not recorded anywhere" with engine identity as the secondary, partially-mitigated gap.

risks.title: No code path anywhere reconstructs or re-evaluates a scan from stored provenance, so 19.1.9 has no procedure to execute
risks.evidence: Grepping tools/, engine/worker/ and backend-api/app/ for replay / reevaluate / re-evaluate / rerun returns only unrelated matches (engine/worker/dispatcher.py:348 about broker retries, engine/tests/test_phase8_drift.py:1308 about drift threads). tools/ops contains backup.py, release_manifest.py, retention_report.py and rotate_encryption_key.py — none reads a provenance record. release_manifest.py:22-27 is explicit that the two concerns are separate: "provenance in this codebase overwhelmingly means *scan evidence* provenance -- the record proving which policy digest evaluated which input digest -- which is a completed, separate concern."
risks.consequence: A Phase 11 verifier is asked to demonstrate 19.1.9. There is no CLI, management command, endpoint or test that takes a scan id and re-derives its results from stored provenance; the only route is bespoke SQL to extract policy_source plus a hand-run `opa eval` for which the required input document does not exist (REPRO-1). The criterion cannot be exercised, only reasoned about.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11 adversarial pass, dimension "Plan item 19.1.9 — a complete scan can be reproduced from stored provenance": survived 3 independent refuters (1 refuting)
risks.refuter_correction: Accurate version: Plan item 19.1.9 ("verify a complete scan can be reproduced from stored provenance") is NOT MET, and the cause is structural rather than a missing tool. engine/worker/tasks.py:879-886 collects the evidence, computes `digest = canonical_digest(collected_data)` and stores only that digest in provenance.input_digest; the collector payload is persisted nowhere (scan_result_factprint holds only declared bool/int/enum scalars per engine/worker/factprint.py:1-16, and Scan.metadata_snapshot is control metadata). A SHA-256 is not invertible, so no CLI, endpoint or test could reproduce a scan from what is stored -- adding replay tooling would not satisfy the item. The half of the chain that IS reproducible is real: provenance.policy_source stores the evaluated Rego verbatim, with policy_digest and opa_version, though it is withheld from every API response (backend-api/app/schemas/provenance.py:59) so reaching it requires direct SQL. Phase 11 did execute this item and recorded the negative result -- docs/compliance/phase-11/traceability-trace.md section 6 ("the chain breaks here") and release-decision.md:168-171 -- and Phase 3 recorded the same gap (docs/compliance/phase-3/README.md:91, 203, 214). Severity low is right for the incremental value: this restates a limitation the handoff already publishes as its headline traceability break. The correct file anchor is engine/worker/tasks.py:884, not tools/ops/release_manifest.py:22.

risks.title: frontend/.env is tracked in git and the .gitignore rules that would exclude it do not apply to an already-tracked file
risks.evidence: `git ls-files` lists frontend/.env; `git check-ignore -v frontend/.env` returns nothing. The root .gitignore lines 28-33 ignore .env, .env.*, **/.env and **/.env.* with an exception only for .env.example, and every other .env in the repository is correctly excluded. frontend/.env is present in the stack base 8736fcb9 and in upstream/main, so it predates those rules.
risks.consequence: A developer adding a value to the file the .gitignore claims to protect commits it. The file is a Vite env file, so VITE_* values are inlined into the production client bundle at build time and reach every browser. Its current content is only VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:8000, so nothing is exposed today; the hazard is that the repository's own secret controls read as covering this file and do not.
risks.verified_by: Phase 11, directly
risks.remedy: `git rm --cached frontend/.env`, or keep it and delete the .gitignore rules that falsely imply it is protected.
